In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of eprinometcin on the levels of nitric oxide in the brain, liver, gills, and plasma of silver catfish.
the effects of the antiparasite eprinomethcin on the NO levels in brain, gill and liver of silver catfish.
the effects of eprinomecin on NOx levels in fish, and is the first study to report NO levels in silver catfish exposed in vivo to eprinomectin, and to evaluate its recovery.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
eprinometcin, a macrocyclic lactone antiparasitic, is toxic to silver catfish at the concentrations evaluated.

the NOx levels were significantly increased at the two highest concentration of eprinometin (1.14 and 1.80 mg/L), and the NOx levels increased in all tissues (brain, liver and gills) of silver catfish after 48 h exposure to eprinometcin.
the NOx levels were not increased in the fish brain, liver, or gill tissue at 24 h of eprinometcin exposure but were increased at 48 h.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NOx levels in organs are good biomarkers to assess the toxic effects of eprinometin on fish.

NOx levels in fish exposed for 48 h to eprinometcin concentrations higher than 1.12 mg/L, and then left for 48 hours of recovery in epprinomectin free, may be used as a biomarker of the inflammatory process caused by epprinomectomy in the organs analyzed.

NO levels are increased in brain, liver and gills of juvenile silver cat fish exposed to eprimomectin for 24 and/or 48h, and that the increase in NO levels is not completely reverted after 48h in water without eprimomctin.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NOx levels in fish organs can be used as a biomarker to detect the presence of eprinometcin in the water.
the use of eprinometcin should not be considered as an alternative to the use of ivermectin for the treatment and control of parasitic diseases in fish.
NO levels in brain, gills and liver of silver catfish can be used as biomarkers of exposure to eprinometin.
